abstract.p: Despite much effort, the molecular mechanisms of retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death remain unclear. To identify common cell death-promoting machinery in the mechanically and chemically injured retina, we profiled temporal gene expression patterns and studied their functional roles in the rodent retina. In response to axotomy and intravitreal NMDA injection, 868 genes were commonly differentially expressed compared with those in normal retinas. K-means clustering assigned those common genes to 5 clusters on the basis of their temporal expression patterns, i.e., early, intermediate and late upregulated gene clusters, and early and late downregulated clusters. Most of the common genes and their assigned canonical pathways and molecular functions in each cluster were shared between axotomy and NMDA, indicating that their temporal expression profiles and functional roles are similar. Some of the common genes, including protein tyrosine phosphatases, formed specific molecular networks. Studies using chemical activators/inhibitors and knockout mice have demonstrated that protein tyrosine phosphatase 1/2 and interleukin-1 beta are detrimental to cell survival, whereas endothelin 2, the proteasome and galanin are neuroprotective. Thus, our integrated time-resolved expression profiling of common genes with bioinformatics and functional validation can help us to better understand the precise molecular mechanisms of RGC survival and death.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Retinal ganglion cell (RGC) death is associated with multiple types of optic neuropathies such as glaucoma and anterior ischemic optic neuropathy. To develop better therapeutic interventions, much effort has focused on understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying RGC death. Earlier studies have identified potential factors that regulate RGC survival and death, which include excitotoxicity, oxidative stress, loss of neurotrophic support, immune dysfunction, neuroinflammation and protein misfolding1–5. Among them, excitotoxicity is one of the most studied hypotheses as a potential cause of glaucoma as well as a therapeutic target for the disease1. Animal studies have reported that glutamate receptor antagonists, including memantine and MK-801, protect RGCs against cell death induced by intravitreal injection of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)6,7, retinal ischemia8,9, a genetic manipulation of glutamate transporter genes10 and ocular hypertension11,12, supporting this hypothesis. However, two identically designed clinical trials demonstrated that oral administration of the NMDA antagonist memantine failed to halt visual field progression in glaucomatous patients13. Although these results do not exclude excitotoxity as a main cause of RGC death in glaucoma, they suggest that simultaneous activation of some of the proposed factors and/or their complex interactions trigger RGC death. Furthermore, different cell death signaling pathways triggered by these initial insults may converge into one shared downstream pathway, because RGCs eventually die via apoptosis in a variety of animal disease models14 and human glaucomatous eyes15,16. In fact, apoptotic signaling is recognized as the common molecular machinery determining the fate of retinal cells17 as well as other types of cells18. Therefore, we hypothesized that a common molecular pathway could exist between primary upstream insults and the final apoptosis execution signals involved in RGC death.

Gene expression profiling via microarrays and RNA sequencing is a powerful technique for unveiling complex transcriptional programs that regulate RGC death19,20. Many studies have successfully identified differentially expressed genes in a variety of animal models of RGC death and subsequently performed bioinformatic analysis to predict their potential biological roles21–24. However, interpretation of those predicted outcomes remains a major challenge because bioinformatic approaches provide only working hypotheses that should be validated in a series of in vitro and in vivo genetic, biochemical and pharmacological experiments. A few investigators have already taken into account this challenge and deployed more integrated approaches in DBA/2J mice25,26, a mouse optic nerve crush model27, microbead-induced ocular hypertensive mice28 and NMDA excitotoxicity in mice29, providing successful examples for functional validation of differentially expressed genes. In particular, through clustering and pathway analysis techniques, the temporal patterns of differentially expressed genes in response to ocular hypertension in DBA2J mice were analyzed, and early upregulated gene clusters, including complement 1q and endothelin 2 genes, were found to precede retinal and optic nerve pathologies25. Importantly, they also demonstrated that genetic and pharmacological manipulations of these identified genes and their products significantly protected optic nerve axons from glaucomatous damage. Thus, this study highlighted that functional validation of unique gene clusters should be integrated with time-resolved gene expression profiling and bioinformatic analysis to gain more insight into the precise molecular mechanisms underlying RGC survival and death.

The present study was designed to identify the common molecular signaling pathway leading to RGC death triggered by 2 different types of retinal insults, namely, optic nerve transection (axotomy) and NMDA. We first obtained the time-resolved profile of retinal gene expression in both animal models via microarrays, which were further analyzed by clustering and pathway analysis to identify a set of functionally relevant genes. We then performed genetic and pharmacological studies to determine the functional roles of these identified genes in RGC death, mainly in the NMDA model. Here, we report that axotomy- and NMDA-induced retinal injury is associated with several common signaling pathways, particularly the protein tyrosine phosphatase network, which may contribute at least partly to RGC survival and death in both retinal injury models.

sec.title: Discovery of genes expressed differentially in response to retinal injury induced by axotomy and NMDA
sec.p: To identify the common pathways leading to RGC death, we profiled temporal patterns of retinal gene expression for 28 days in each retinal injury model (see Supplementary Fig. S1 for the study design), namely, axotomy (normal control, sham-operation and axotomy) and NMDA (normal control, phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) as a vehicle and 20 nmol/eye NMDA intravitreal injection). We first performed preliminary statistical analysis via one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with the Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate method30. This analysis yielded 288 and 1,539 differentially expressed genes in the axotomized and NMDA-injected retinas, respectively, when compared between day 0 in the normal control group and all the other designated time points in each retinal injury group. Among all differentially expressed genes, 215 genes overlapped between both groups (Supplementary Data File 1), 32 and 26% of which were reported in earlier studies using rat axotomy31 and mouse NMDA models29, respectively. However, this approach failed to detect many of the differentially expressed genes found in those studies, including biologically significant genes such as Il1b, Jag1 and Il6r, which reached statistical significance via individual multiple comparisons (ANOVA followed by Dunnett’s test, Supplementary Fig. S2 and Supplementary Table S1). Therefore, we used conventional ANOVA without the false discovery rate correction for further data analysis below to increase the likelihood to identify biologically significant genes associated with RGC survival and death.

Among the 20,500 genes detected by microarray, even in normal eyes, 478 and 736 retinal genes were differentially expressed on day 28 in the axotomy experiment (Fig. 1a) and the NMDA experiment (Fig. 1b), respectively, compared with day 0. In the sham-operated and vehicle-injected eyes, 1,378 and 700 differentially expressed genes, respectively, were found when all 3 designated time points (6 h, days 7 and 28) were compared with those of the normal group on day 0. Similarly, 1,534 and 3,242 genes were differentially expressed in the axotomized and NMDA-injected eyes, respectively, when compared between normal day 0 and all 7 designated time points (6 and 12 h and days 1, 3, 7, 14 and 28). As shown in Figs. 1a and b, 80 and 584 differentially expressed genes overlapped between the axotomy group and the normal or sham-operation groups, respectively, whereas 305 and 393 genes overlapped between the NMDA-injection group and the respective control group. When all the differentially expressed genes were compared between the axotomy and NMDA groups (Fig. 1c), 838 genes overlapped and were designated as common genes for further analysis. Gene expression was also altered even in the fellow intact eyes (1,068 and 1,393 genes in the axotomy and NMDA groups, respectively), and 508 and 894 genes overlapped between the injured and intact eyes in the axotomy and NMDA groups, respectively (Supplementary Fig. S3).

caption.p: Venn diagrams for differentially expressed genes in the axotomized (optic nerve transection) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)-injected rat retinas. Total RNA was extracted from 3 to 8 retinas combined at each time point in the respective groups of axotomized and NMDA (20 nmol/eye)-injected eyes, and the resulting fluorescein-labeled cRNA was hybridized to rat oligo microarrays. In the sham-operation and vehicle injection groups, eyes received ocular surgery without optic nerve transection and vehicle injection (phosphate-buffered saline), respectively, whereas those in the normal control group were left intact in both experiments. Three independent microarray experiments were performed using the same pooled RNA samples. To determine differentially expressed genes, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed for differences between values obtained on day 0 in the respective normal groups and those at the remaining time points (6 and 12 h, and 1, 3, 7, 14 and 28 days) in each group (P < 0.05). (a) Numbers of unique and shared genes in axotomized, sham-operated and normal retinas, and (b) in NMDA-injected, vehicle-injected and normal retinas. (c) All differentially expressed genes in either the axotomy group or the NMDA group compared with those on day 0 in the normal group were used to determine the genes shared between the two groups and were defined as commonly regulated genes (common genes).

sec.p: For all 838 common genes, we first performed unbiased two-dimensional hierarchical clustering to detect any data variabilities particularly among 3 replicates in each individual time point in the axotomy and NMDA datasets (Supplementary Fig. S4). In all groups, 3 replicates were tightly clustered and placed next to each other. This clustering also showed the distinct expression patterns of upregulated and downregulated genes between early and later time points. Next, we further analyzed the temporal gene expression profiles via unbiased one-dimensional clustering for gene entities with fixed time points in both datasets. As shown in Fig. 2 (upper panel), we could detect the more distinct temporal gene expression patterns, resulting in identification of at least 3 upregulated and 2 downregulated gene clusters via dendrograms and visual inspection. To minimize a potential bias by visual inspection, we finally performed k-means clustering to assign the time-resolved expression profiles to 12 gene clusters in the axotomy and NMDA datasets (Fig. 2, lower panel). These 12 clusters were further arbitrarily grouped into 5 combined clusters on the basis of their temporal expression patterns: early (early up), intermediate (intermediate up), and late upregulated clusters (late up) and early (early down) and late downregulated clusters (late down). In the axotomy dataset (Fig. 2, lower-left panel), the early up cluster included the genes upregulated immediately and transiently after axotomy (106 genes in cluster 11) and those with this initial response followed by the second upregulation phase (40 genes in cluster 7 and 97 genes in cluster 8). In the intermediate up cluster (174 in clusters 1, 5 and 9), the genes presented similar temporal expression patterns to those in the early up cluster, but their onset was relatively slow. The genes in the late up cluster (140 genes in clusters 4 and 2) started to change at a later time point and continued to increase gradually throughout the experimental period. The early down (73 genes) and late down clusters (208 genes) included rapid-onset and sustainably downregulated genes (clusters 10 and 3) and slow-onset and progressively downregulated genes (clusters 0 and 6), respectively. Generally, the differentially expressed genes in the NMDA dataset (Fig. 2, lower-right panel) were also grouped into 5 combined clusters in the same manner (early up: 248 genes in clusters 1, 7 and 4; intermediate up: 161 genes in clusters 10, 8 and 3; late up: 176 genes in clusters 2 and 11; early down: 67 genes in clusters 9 and 5; late down: 186 genes in clusters 6 and 0). Detailed gene expression and clustering data for the common genes are available in Supplementary Data File 1.

caption.p: One-dimensional hierarchical and k-means clustering for the temporal expression profile of commonly regulated genes in response to axotomy (optic nerve transection)- and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)-induced retinal injury. Upper panel: hierarchical clustering was performed only for gene entities with fixed time points. The resulting clusters of the common genes depicted in Fig. 1c were visually inspected and grouped into 5 major clusters, i.e., early (red rectangle), intermediate (orange) and late upregulated gene clusters (yellow), and early (light blue) and late downregulated gene clusters (dark blue) in the axotomy (Axo, a) and NMDA datasets (b). Color codes as shown on the upper-right corner represent the expression level of each gene. Lower panel: k-means clustering was performed for the common genes, which were arbitrarily assigned to 12 clusters and further grouped into 3 combined clusters for upregulated genes (early, intermediate and late upregulated gene clusters) and 2 clusters for downregulated genes (early down and late downregulated gene clusters), on the basis of their visually inspected temporal gene expression patterns. Each value represents the average expression level of all differentially expressed genes assigned to the respective cluster. The number of genes in each cluster is shown in parentheses. Each gene expression value was normalized to that obtained on day 0 in the normal (Nor) group and expressed as log2 ratios. The representative genes are shown in each hierarchical and k-means cluster (arrows and/or gene names). Note that gene expression values for the sham, vehicle and normal groups were excluded from this analysis, except for those obtained on day 0 in the normal group.

sec.p: As shown in Fig. 3a, the axotomy and NMDA datasets shared more than 80% of the commonly upregulated genes (88.7% in axotomy and 83.6% in NMDA), but this number varied from 42.7 to 71.9% in individual combined clusters. As expected, some genes were found in the same clusters in both datasets, e.g., Mapk14, Mmp3 and Hmox1 in the early up clusters (Fig. 3b); Psmb9, Lgals3 and Fkbp1a in the intermediate up clusters (Fig. 3c); and Ca2, Myoc, Tf and Ttr in the late up clusters (Fig. 3d). Unlike these genes, several other genes were assigned to clusters next to each other (Cntf, Gal and Prss 56, Drd4 and Lgmn; Figs. 3b-d). The axotomy and NMDA datasets also shared commonly downregulated genes, but the percentages of the shared genes were lower than those in the upregulation clusters (62.9% in axotomy and 73.0% in NMDA, Figs. 3a, e and f). In particular, the rate of the shared genes in the early down clusters was the lowest (24.1% in axotomy and 26.4% in NMDA), although those in the late down clusters were comparable to those in the remaining clusters. Interestingly, a small fraction of the common genes were differentially regulated between the axotomy and NMDA datasets (Fig. 3g). For example, the Atf3, Jun and Cebpg genes were upregulated in the axotomy dataset but downregulated in the NMDA dataset, whereas the Ccng, Pax 4 and Runx 1 genes were downregulated in the axotomy dataset but upregulated in the NMDA dataset. Thus, the time-resolved expression profiles of the common genes were similar between the 2 different types of retinal injury, although they were not identical.

caption.p: Unique and shared genes in all combined gene clusters in the axotomy (optic nerve transection) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) datasets. (a) The number of genes in each combined cluster is shown in bar graphs (open bar: unique; black bar: shared genes) with the percentages of the shared genes. All upregulated gene clusters combined the genes assigned to early, intermediate and late upregulated gene clusters, whereas all downregulated clusters combined those assigned to early and late downregulated gene clusters. (b-f) Temporal expression patterns of representative genes in early (b), intermediate (c) and late upregulated gene clusters (d) and early (e) and late downregulated gene clusters (f). (g) Temporal expression patterns of the genes regulated reciprocally between the axotomy and NMDA datasets. Notably, the Atf3 gene was upregulated in the axotomy dataset, whereas it was downregulated in the NMDA dataset. Each gene expression value was normalized to that obtained on day 0 in the normal group and expressed as log2 ratios. Each value represents the average of those in 3 independent hybridizations. See Supplementary Data File 1 for more information about each listed gene.

sec.p: To confirm the reproducibility of gene expression measured via microarrays, we performed real-time PCR for 9 genes that were arbitrarily selected among the common genes between the axotomy and NMDA datasets. Figures 4a (axotomy) and b (NMDA) show the time course of changes in the expression of 4 representative genes (Tnfrsf1a, Gfap, C3 and Nefl). The temporal patterns of gene expression obtained with microarrays and real-time PCR were superimposed for most of the tested genes, although the magnitude of changes in the expression of some genes was different between these 2 techniques (e.g., Gfap). When all the quantitative data for the 9 genes obtained at each designated time point were plotted in each retinal injury model (Fig. 4c), a strong correlation was observed between the changes in gene expression measured via microarrays and real-time PCR in the axotomy (R2 = 0.93, P < 0.0001) and NMDA datasets (R2 = 0.84, P < 0.0001). Thus, our microarray-based gene expression profiling was reliable and warranted further functional annotation.

caption.p: Comparison of time-resolved gene expression profiles determined by microarray (array) and real-time PCR (qPCR) in the axotomy (optic nerve transection) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) groups. (a and b) Four representative genes (Tnfrsf1a: TNF receptor superfamily member 1 A; Gfap: glial fibrillary acidic protein; C3: complement component 3; Nefl: neurofilament light chain) were selected for this comparison (open circle: array; closed circle: qPCR) in the axotomy (a) and NMDA groups (b). Each gene expression value was normalized to that obtained on day 0 in the normal group and expressed as log2 ratios. Each value represents the average of those in 3 independent hybridizations or qPCR experiments. (c) Scatter plots of the expression levels of 9 selected genes determined by microarray and qPCR. All data obtained at each time point are included in both scatter plots in the axotomy (upper) and NMDA groups (lower), and linear regression analysis yields the respective equations and R square values.

sec.title: Functional annotation of the genes commonly regulated in axotomy- and NMDA-induced retinal injury
sec.p: To gain more insight into the functional roles of the common genes in RGC death, we performed gene annotation via the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA) software32, which mapped 697 common genes in its database called the Ingenuity Pathways Knowledge Base (PKB). First, we analyzed the molecular features of the common genes in each designated cluster (Fig. 5 and Supplementary Fig. S5). In all combined clusters, the major identified molecular features were transcriptional regulators, transporters and enzymes, followed by peptidases and kinases. Regardless of the number of genes, some molecular features presented their unique distribution patterns across all combined clusters. For example, cytokine genes appeared mainly in the early and intermediate up clusters but not often in the remaining clusters in both the axotomy and NMDA datasets, although the number of genes was quite small (Fig. 5, top panel). Similar patterns were observed for the majority of the other molecular features, namely, growth factors, transmembrane receptors, peptidases, kinases, phosphatases, transcription regulators and translation regulators (Fig. 5, top and middle panels). For the remaining features (Fig. 5, bottom panel), G protein-coupled receptor and ion channel genes appeared most frequently in the intermediate and late up clusters and the late down cluster, whereas transporters and enzymes did not present any specific distribution patterns (see Supplementary Data File 1 for more detailed gene annotation data).

caption.p: Molecular annotation of commonly regulated genes in each combined gene cluster in the axotomy (optic nerve transection) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) datasets. A list of the common genes in each dataset was uploaded into Ingenuity Pathway Analysis software and mapped to the relevant gene objects in the Ingenuity Pathways Knowledge Base. The relevant molecular features were retrieved as indicated at the top of each panel, and the number of genes assigned to each molecular feature was determined in early (early), intermediate (intermediate) and late upregulated gene clusters (late), and early (early down) and late downregulated gene clusters (late down) in the axotomy (black bar) and NMDA groups (gray bar).

sec.p: Next, we further analyzed the common genes associated with predefined canonical pathways and selected the top 5 annotated pathways in each combined cluster on the basis of statistical significance for enrichment of the relevant genes (Fig. 6). As shown in Fig. 6a, the common genes in the early up clusters in the axotomy and NMDA datasets were associated with the same top 3 canonical pathways. Their designated names in IPA were Role of chondrocytes in rheumatoid arthritis signaling, Osteoarthritis, and ID1 signaling, in which both datasets shared 58.3 to 70.0% of the assigned genes. The late up clusters (Fig. 6c) were also associated with the same top 4 clusters: Visual phototransduction, Phototransduction, Erythrocytes take up oxygen and release carbon dioxide, and Erythrocytes take up carbon dioxide and release oxygen, in which 66.7 to 100% of the assigned genes were shared between the 2 datasets. Similarly, in the late down cluster (Fig. 6e), all the top 5 canonical pathways overlapped between both datasets, in which all the assigned genes were shared, and were associated with cholesterol biosynthesis. For the remaining combined clusters, the canonical pathways were diverse and completely different between the axotomy and NMDA datasets, except for Antigen presentation pathway in the intermediate up cluster (Figs. 6b and d).

caption.p: Canonical pathways associated with commonly regulated genes in each combined gene cluster in the axotomy (optic nerve transection) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) datasets. The common genes in each dataset were analyzed via Ingenuity Pathway Analysis software as described in Fig. 5. The relevant pathways were retrieved with statistical significance (-logP values), and the number of genes assigned to each pathway was determined in early (a), intermediate (b) and late upregulated gene clusters (c), and early (d) and late downregulated gene clusters (e) in each dataset. The number of unique and shared genes in each combined cluster is shown in bar graphs (open bar: unique; black bar: shared genes), and the shared genes are listed only for overlapping pathways between two datasets. A right-tailed Fisher’s exact test was performed, and statistical significance was considered if P < 0.05. For each cluster, the top 5 canonical pathways associated statistically significantly with the common genes were chosen for visualization.

sec.p: Finally, the top 5 predefined molecular and cellular functions were assigned to the common genes in each combined cluster (Fig. 7). All combined clusters included 2 to 4 overlapping molecular and cellular functions between the axotomy and NMDA datasets, with 0 to 85.7% shared genes in the respective functions. Cellular development and Cell death and survival overlapped among most of the combined clusters (Figs. 7a-d), whereas Cell growth and proliferation, Gene expression, and Cell-to-cell signaling and interaction were unique to the early up (Fig. 7a) and intermediate up clusters (Fig. 7b), respectively. Lipid metabolism and Small molecule biochemistry also overlapped between the late up (Fig. 7c) and late down clusters (Fig. 7e), whereas Vitamin and mineral metabolism and Cellular assembly and organization were the unique features in the late down cluster (Fig. 7e). All the identified canonical pathways and molecular and cellular functions in each cluster are listed in Supplementary Data File 2.

caption.p: Molecular and cellular functions associated with commonly regulated genes in each combined gene cluster in the axotomy (optic nerve transection) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) datasets. The common genes in each dataset were analyzed via Ingenuity Pathway Analysis software as described in Fig. 5. The relevant functions were retrieved with statistical significance (-logP values), and the number of genes assigned to each function was determined in early (a), intermediate (b) and late upregulated gene clusters (c), and early (d) and late downregulated gene clusters (e) in each dataset. Note that the range of statistical significance is presented for each function, because molecular and cellular functions comprise several subcategories. See Fig. 6 for more details.

sec.p: Taken together, regardless of the nature of primary insults, retinal injury may trigger the same cellular responses comprising cellular development and cell survival and death signaling possibly via immunoregulatory processes, eventually leading to impaired cellular metabolism and structural maintenance.

sec.title: Putative interactions among the common genes involved in axotomy- and NMDA-induced retinal injury
sec.p: To further explore the molecular interactions among the common genes in each combined cluster, we generated more specific networks among the individual common genes in each combined cluster of the axotomy and NMDA datasets. The networks ranked in the top 5 for each cluster were selected on the basis of their scores and are shown in Figs. 8a and b and Supplementary Figs. S6-11. In the early up clusters, protein kinase and phosphatase (network 2, Fig. 8 and Supplementary Fig. S6), RNA posttranscriptional (network 3, Supplementary Fig. S7), kinesin and microtubule (network 4, Supplementary Fig. S7), and Cd47 (network 2 in axotomy and network 5 in NMDA, Supplementary Figs. S6 and 7) networks, including some of the common genes, overlapped between the axotomy and NMDA datasets. Protein kinase and phosphatase-network 2 (Fig. 8) was also associated with the Smad3 network linked to S1pr3 and other molecules, including Adamts1 and Anxa7 in the axotomy dataset and Cxcl10 and Gal in the NMDA dataset. Notably, the cytokine and growth factor network, including Il1b, Litaf, Tnfrsf1a, Cntf and Mapk14, was found in network 1 in the axotomy dataset, and a similar network, including Il1b, Il6st, Il6r, Mmp3, Pdgfa, and Stat1, was found in network 8 in the NMDA dataset (Supplementary Fig. S7).

caption.p: Putative molecular networks among commonly regulated genes in each combined gene cluster in the axotomy (optic nerve transection, a) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) datasets (b). The common genes in each dataset were analyzed via Ingenuity Pathway Analysis software as described in Fig. 5. A right-tailed Fisher’s exact test was performed for the enrichment of a group of genes in a given network and statistical significance was considered if P < 0.05. For each cluster, the top 5 networks associated statistically significantly with the common genes were chosen on the basis of their scores, and only one network shared between both datasets is shown with their scores in parentheses. See Supplementary Figs. S6-11 for detailed information, including the legends and symbols.

sec.p: For the intermediate up clusters, the major overlapping networks were antigen presentation (network 3 in axotomy and network 1 in NMDA, Fig. 8 and Supplementary Fig. S6) and complement pathways (network 4 in axotomy and network 2 in NMDA, Supplementary Fig. S8). Axotomy-antigen presentation network 3 was further linked to Lgals3, Fcgr2a, Anxa2, Vcam1, and Cd47 (Fig. 8), and NMDA-complement network 2 was linked to a similar Lgals3 network, including Lgals1, Anxa2, Prss23, Fn1, A2m and Sdc1 (Supplementary Fig. S8). Additionally, axotomy-complement network 4 was associated with the broader network comprising Stat1, A2m, Sdc1, Mmp14, Hspa5, and Psmb9, some of which were also found in NMDA network3 (Supplementary Fig. S8). The axotomy and NMDA late up clusters shared the same networks formed among the genes related to transferrin-transthyretin (network 1 in axotomy and network 2 in NMDA, Fig. 8 and Supplementary Fig. S6), laminin-collagen (network 1, Fig. 8 and Supplementary Fig. S9), retinal G-protein coupled receptor (network 1, Fig. 8 and Supplementary Fig. S9), heat shock protein (network 2, Fig. 8, Supplementary Fig. S9), and estrogen (network 4 in axotomy and network 3 in NMDA, Supplementary Fig. S9). Axotomy network 1 also included cysteine proteases and their inhibitors (Cst3 and Lgmn) and complement pathways (Fig. 8) similar to axotomy network 4 in the intermediate up cluster (Supplementary Fig. S8). NMDA network 2 was further linked to another G-protein network, including Drd4, Grp37 and Cst3 (Fig. 8) and a similar network was also found in axotomy network 2, including Cxcl10 and Gal, in the intermediate up cluster (Supplementary Fig. S8).

Only one network among various crystallin genes overlapped in the early down clusters between the axotomy and NMDA datasets (network 1, Fig. 8 and Supplementary Figs. S6 and 10). In the late down clusters, the shared networks were related to the genes regulating neurofilaments (network 5 in axotomy and network 2 in NMDA, Fig. 8 and Supplementary Fig. S6) and neuronal signal transduction (network 2 in axotomy and network 1 in NMDA, Supplementary Fig. S11). All the identified molecular networks in each cluster are listed in Supplementary Data File 3.

sec.title: Functional validation of target genes using knockout mice and small chemical activators and inhibitors
sec.p: Pathway analysis revealed several interesting molecular networks among the common genes, suggesting their functional roles in retinal cell survival and death. To test this hypothesis, we focused on the commonly upregulated genes, because their temporal profiles were more consistent between the axotomy and NMDA datasets, and downregulation may be simply due to impaired neuronal functions and/or loss of neuronal cells following axotomy- and NMDA-induced retinal injury. One of the most promising networks was related to immune functions and inflammation, including cytokine and growth factor networks, antigen presentation and complement pathways (Fig. 8 and Supplementary Figs. S6-8). Therefore, we first examined whether these pathways might be involved in NMDA-induced retinal injury in 5 knockout mice (Figs. 9 and 10) with homozygous deletion of Il1b (early up cluster), Fcgr3 (a mouse ortholog of rat Fcgr2a, intermediate up cluster), B2m (intermediate up cluster), H2-Ab1 (Abb, a mouse ortholog of rat RT1-Bb as a proxy for RT1-Ba, intermediate up cluster), C3 (late up cluster in axotomy and intermediate up cluster in NMDA), and 1 transgenic mouse with constitutively active Gp130 signaling (early up cluster). As shown in Figs. 9 and 10 (see Supplementary Fig. S12 for individual data points), intravitreal injection of NMDA (10 and 20 nmol/eye) resulted in cell loss in the ganglion cell layer (GCL) and the reduced thickness of the inner plexiform layer (IPL), as shown in our previous studies33. Surprisingly, none of the tested knockout mice exhibited neuroprotection against NMDA-induced retinal injury, except for Il1b-knockout mice. In Il1b-knockout mice, the degree of neuroprotection was quite mild when two doses of NMDA were tested: only cell loss in the GCL and IPL thinning were slightly lower in mice receiving 10 and 20 nmol/eye NMDA injections, respectively, than in wild-type mice, although these differences between wild-type and knockout mice were statistically significant (P = 0.0365 in cell loss and P = 0.0247 in IPL thinning, Fig. 9a). In Gp130 transgenic mice (Fig. 9b) and Fcgr3 knockout mice (Fig. 9c), the degree of NMDA-induced retinal injury was comparable to that of the respective wild-type mice (on both days 7 and 14 following NMDA injection in Fcgr3 knockout mice). Similarly, NMDA-induced retinal injury was not altered in B2m, Abb and C3 knockout mice compared with their respective wild-type mice (Figs. 10a-c and 20 nmol/eye NMDA were tested in C3 knockout mice).

On days 7 (only for Fcgr3) and 14 following 10 or 20 nmol/eye (only for Il1b) NMDA injection into the left eye (the right eye remained uninjected and was served as a control), the retinas were isolated, cross-sectioned and stained with hematoxylin and eosin. sec.p: On the basis of the identified molecular networks and the findings reported in earlier studies20,27,29,31,34, we expanded the list of targeted common genes in the upregulated gene clusters and further examined their functional roles in NMDA-induced rat retinal injury via the use of small chemical activators and inhibitors available from commercial sources (Supplementary Tables S1 and 2). As shown in Fig. 11a, we first tested 13 target genes via 16 different activators and inhibitors. In this study, NMDA (10 nmol/eye)-induced RGC death was determined via real-time PCR-based quantification of Nefl gene expression, an RGC marker, as reported previously7,35. This functional analysis identified suramin (5 nmol/eye, PTPN1 and 2 inhibitor) and ML3403 (16 nmol/eye), SB202190 (45 nmol/eye) and SB239083 (2.95 nmol/eye, MAPK14 inhibitors) as neuroprotective agents, and N-N-diethylspermine tetrahydrochloride (5 nmol/eye, SAT inhibitor), lactacystin (10 nmol/eye) and MG-262 (0.27 nmol/eye, proteasome inhibitors) as neurotoxic agents. To validate these findings and further expand the list of target genes, we examined the effects of activators and inhibitors for 23 target genes, including 16 additional targets, on NMDA (10 and 20 nmol/eye)-induced retinal injury via histological analysis (Fig. 11b and Supplementary Figs. S13-15). As shown in Fig. 11b, this analysis confirmed the neuroprotective effects of suramin and identified two additional compounds as potential neuroprotective agents, namely, sarafotoxin S6c (0.1 nmol/eye, an endothelin receptor B agonist) and propagylglycine (10 nmol/eye, an MT1 and 2 synthesis inhibitor). These and additional positive findings of the histological analysis along with the temporal gene expression patterns are summarized in Fig. 12 (see Supplementary Figs. S13 and 14 for individual data points). Intravitreal injection of the galanin receptor antagonist galanin(1–3)-bradykinin(2–9)amide (M35,10 nmol/eye, Fig. 12a) and the proteasome inhibitor MG-262 (0.1 nmol/eye, Fig. 12b) exacerbated NMDA (20 nmol/eye)-induced inner retinal injury, while preserving the intact outer retinal layer. In contrast, 0.1 nmol/eye sarafotoxin S6c protected the retina against NMDA (20 nmol/eye)-induced injury (Fig. 12c), but this effect was statistically significant only for the IPL thickness (P = 0.0039, Fig. 12e). Suramin (5 nmol/eye) significantly reduced cell loss in the GCL (P < 0.0001, Fig. 12f) but did not affect IPL damage induced by NMDA (10 mol/eye). Interestingly, suramin also exhibited neuroprotection against cell loss induced by optic nerve crush (P < 0.0001), as shown by the use of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF, 2 µg/eye, P = 0.0283) as a positive control, whereas the NMDA receptor antagonist memantine (100 nmol/eye) had no protective effect. Unlike the other two neuroprotectants, the neuroprotective effects of propagylglycine did not reach statistical significance (Fig. 12g), although the cell number in the GCL and the IPL thickness were different between vehicle- and reagent-treated eyes. Consistent with the results in knockout mice, a small chemical C3 inhibitor (1.25 nmol/eye, compstatin, Fig. 11a) or anti-C3 antibody (5 µg/eye, Supplemental Figure S15) did not alter NMDA-induced retinal injury. Furthermore, the complement activator zymosan (50 µg/eye), interferon (INF) gamma (5 ng/eye) or its neutralizing antibody (0.5 µg/eye) did not cause either retinal damage or protection (Supplementary Fig. S15).

sec.p: Thus, 3 death-causing genes (Il1b, Ptpn1 and 2) and 3 neuroprotective genes (Edn2, Psmb9 and Gal) were found to play roles in retinal damage induced by NMDA and possibly optic nerve crush, and most of them were included in the early up clusters in both datasets, suggesting the functional significance of these clusters in mechanically and chemically induced retinal injury.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In the present study, we hypothesized that there could be a converging point leading to neuronal cell death, at which different insults activate common cell death-promoting pathways, regardless of the nature of the primary insults that trigger cell death processes. To test this hypothesis, we generated time-resolved gene expression profiles in the whole retina of mechanically and chemically induced retinal injury models. We found that 838 genes were differentially expressed and overlapped between these two models. Hierarchical and k-means clustering and subsequent gene annotation analysis demonstrated that the temporal expression patterns of these common genes and their predicted molecular functions were very similar between the groups, resulting in the identification of unique molecular networks potentially associated with RGC death. In fact, our functional validation of the genes selected from these networks demonstrated that their inhibitors and activators could either exacerbate or prevent NMDA-induced retinal damage, underscoring their roles as cell death machinery or intrinsic neuroprotective mechanisms via transcriptional regulation. Thus, our time-resolved gene expression profiling integrated with bioinformatic analysis and functional validation provides more insight into the precise molecular mechanisms underlying retinal cell survival and death.

Although gene expression profiles have extensively been studied particularly in high intraocular pressure (IOP), axotomy and optic nerve crush models19,20, our study design was unique in three major points: First, we chose two authentic animal models, namely, axotomy- and NMDA-induced retinal injury to identify commonly regulated genes. Only a few studies36,37 have directly compared comprehensive gene expression profiles between high IOP and axotomy/optic nerve crush, but not NMDA-induced retinal injury yet. Unlike high IOP models, their clinical relevance to human ocular diseases remains unsolved. However, their experimental procedures are simple and easy to repeat, and the results obtained from earlier studies are consistent and reproducible among different investigators and laboratories7,27,29,38–40. Second, our gene expression profiles were generated at high temporal resolution using 7 time points for axotomized and NMDA-injected, 3 time points for sham-operated and vehicle-injected, and 2 time points for normal control eyes, respectively. Comparable time-resolved gene expression profiles have been reported only in a limited number of earlier studies in either high IOP25,36 or axotomy/optic nerve crush models27,36,41. As shown in our study, this level of temporal resolution is crucial in acquiring the dynamic temporal changes in gene expression in these retinal injury models. Finally, we employed hierarchical and k-means clustering and molecular network analysis for the temporal expression profiles of commonly regulated genes between axotomy and NMDA. An earlier study via k-means clustering and pathway analysis successfully found early molecular events associated with RGC survival and death in DBA/2J ocular hypertensive mice25. Similarly, we identified via similar analysis methods 32 candidate genes, which may be associated with the common cell-death promoting pathways following different primary insults. To detect differentially expressed genes, we used conventional ANOVA without Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate method30, which has frequently been used in earlier studies28,34,42, because we realized that this method could not detect some biologically significant genes tested for our functional validation. Our identified genes (697 genes annotated in IPA out of 838) overlapped with those in earlier studies in a rat optic nerve crush model31, a mouse optic nerve crush model27 and a mouse NMDA model29 by 30% (208 genes), 16% (110 genes) and 24% (170 genes), respectively. Given differences in experimental conditions such as transcriptomic analysis technologies, temporal resolution and animal species, this level of consistency seems to be reasonable as summarized in an earlier review article20.

Axotomy and NMDA trigger different primary molecular events leading to retinal cell death: axotomy disturbs the retrograde transport of neurotrophic factors to RGC somata2, whereas NMDA causes calcium overload to retinal cells via the activation of inotropic glutamate receptors43. Regardless of the initial molecular events, they undergo apoptosis as the final cell death execution mechanism14, suggesting that common intermediate cell death-promoting machinery leads to apoptosis. In this study, we found that the temporal expression patterns of the common genes were concordant between the axotomy and NMDA datasets. In particular, more than 80% of the genes overlapped in the upregulated clusters, which comprised genes with a variety of molecular features, such as cytokines, growth factors, kinases and phosphatases, that were found predominantly in the early up clusters. In these clusters, many of these genes were associated with canonical pathways related to immune responses and inflammation and with molecular functions, including cell death and survival. Furthermore, their assigned genes formed individual molecular networks, such as protein tyrosine phosphatases and IL-1 signaling pathways. These results suggest that the common cell death-promoting mechanism actively operates immediately after retinal injury triggered by axotomy and NMDA, possibly via altered local immune functions, as proposed in earlier studies21,29,44. In contrast, the overlapping genes in the downregulated clusters, particularly those in the late down clusters, were associated with ion channels, neuronal signal transduction and metabolic processes, suggesting that passive processes reflect impaired retinal neuronal functions and/or structural integrity secondary to the cellular damage induced by axotomy and NMDA. On the basis of this network analysis, we chose 32 genes mainly in the upregulated clusters for functional validation (Supplementary Tables S1 and 2). Out of 32 genes, 20 have not been functionally validated yet in an axotomy, optic nerve crush or NMDA model. Our functional validation successfully identified several potential genes regulating cell survival and death in axotomy- and NMDA-induced retinal injury, although the number of genes tested was only 5–6% of all commonly upregulated genes (557 and 585 genes in axotomy and NMDA datasets, respectively).

One of our major findings was that we identified the protein kinase and phosphatase network formed among the common genes, including Ptpn1 and 2, in the early up clusters in both retinal injury models. In earlier studies, Ptpn1, but not Ptpn2, was also reported to be upregulated in response to both axotomy and optic nerve crush31, whereas both genes remained unchanged in NMDA-injected eyes29. Interestingly, the protein tyrosine phosphatase inhibitor suramin significantly prevented NMDA-induced cellular damage. We also confirmed that suramin exhibited neuroprotection against cell loss due to optic nerve crush, which was comparable to that of BDNF. Suramin nonselectively inhibits the activity of various phosphatases such as PTPN1 and CDC25A45,46. Ptpn1 is ubiquitously expressed in the retina, including RGCs47, whereas the retinal localization of Ptpn2 remains unknown. PTPN1 activity was shown to be increased in multiple mouse models of retinal degeneration. These include the rhodopsin mutant, Rpe65 knockout and streptozotocin-induced diabetic retinopathy47,48. While reducing retinal PTPN1 activity, light stress causes retinal degeneration, which is suppressed by photoreceptor-specific Ptpn1 knockout and intravitreal injection of another PTP inhibitor, suggesting a role for light-mediated suppression of PTPN1 activity as an intrinsic retinal protective mechanism48. Furthermore, intravitreal injection of PTPN2 chemical inhibitors or its conditional knockout in RGCs was reported to promote the axonal regeneration capacities of RGCs following optic nerve crush in mice, which were augmented by low dose INF gamma treatment49. Thus, our study extends these earlier findings to an additional role for Ptpn1 in regulating RGC death induced by NMDA and optic nerve crush. Given that suramin has a variety of pharmacological actions other than PTPN1 inhibition50, one might argue that the observed retinal protective effect of suramin could be due to PTPN1-unrelated off-target actions. Among them, one of the most important off-target actions of suramin is NMDA receptor antagonism51. However, this possibility can be denied partly by the fact that suramin significantly prevents optic nerve crush-induced cellular loss in the GCL, which is resistant to the authentic NMDA receptor antagonist memantine. Thus, it is likely that Ptpn1, and possibly Ptpn2, may play key roles as a common cell death-promoting pathway leading to apoptosis in both optic nerve crush and NMDA.

Our study revealed another important molecular interaction shared between the axotomy and NMDA groups in the upregulated clusters, which was associated with the cytokine and growth factor network. This finding is consistent with the proposed roles of the immune system in RGC death in glaucoma25,52 and traumatic retinal and optic nerve injury models21,37,42. Collectively, these findings suggest that these changes in gene expression reflect the activation of microglia, astrocytes and/or Müller glia in the retina and optic nerve, leading to axonal damage and RGC death19,20,53. Consistently, we found that microglial28,54 (Gpnmb, Spp1, Lgals3 and Cd63) and astrocyte/Müller glial activation marker genes42 (Gfap, S100, Anxa5, Clu and Cntf) were upregulated in response to axotomy and NMDA. The cytokine and growth factor network included Il1b, Cntf, Tnfrsf1a, Odc1 and Mapk14 in the axotomy dataset (network 1), and Il1b, Il6r, Il6st and Mmp3 in the NMDA dataset (network 8), although all genes were upregulated in both datasets. Genetic ablation of the Il1b gene only slightly, but statistically significantly, suppressed NMDA-induced retinal damage, whereas genetic manipulation (Il6r and Il6st), antibodies (Cntf and Tnfsf1a) or chemical inhibitors (Il6r and Il6st, Tnfrsf1a, Odc1, Mapk14 and Mmp3) of the remaining genes (and their encoded proteins) did not alter it. Thus, our functional validation using knockout mice, small chemical inhibitors and neutralizing antibodies demonstrated that any genes in these shared networks, with the exception of Il1b, may not contribute directly to NMDA-induced cellular damage, as the common cell death-promoting machinery does.

Surprisingly, we could not find any supportive evidence for the roles of complement or antigen presentation related factors in axotomy- or NMDA-induced retinal damage. In both models, the genes in the intermediate up (network 4 in axotomy and network 2 in NMDA) and late up (network 1 in axotomy) clusters formed complement pathway networks along with the antigen presentation network (network 3 in axotomy and network 1 in NMDA). For those genes, genetic deletion (Fcgr2a, B2m, Abb and C3), antibodies (C3 and Infg) or chemical activators/inhibitors (RT1-Ba, C3, Lgals1 and 3, Prss23 and C1s) did not prevent NMDA-induced retinal cell loss. Although our findings seem to contradict the proposed RGC death-promoting roles of immune modulators, including complement factors, cytokines and antigen presentation, their exact biological functions in retinal neuronal survival and death are still controversial55,56. For example, earlier studies on the roles of complement factors in RGC death provided conflicting results: deficiency of C1q, C3ar1 or C5 prevented RGC axonal degeneration25,57,58 and cellular loss induced by IOP elevation59, whereas that of C3 did not rescue RGCs in an optic nerve crush60 or motor neurons in SOD mutant ALS models61and C3 itself could even be protective against RGC axonal degeneration induced by IOP elevation62. Similarly, TNF-alpha reportedly mediates RGC death induced by chronic IOP elevation63–65 and NMDA excitotoxicity29. These findings are inconsistent with those of other studies showing that TNF-alpha protects RGCs against cell death induced by optic nerve crush66 and transection67 and does not contribute to NMDA-induced retinal damage40. This discrepancy suggests that the roles of complement factors and cytokines in retinal neuronal survival and death depend on the nature, degree and timing of cell death induced by various retinal insults. Taken together, the cytokine and growth factor, complement and antigen presentation networks may not be major determinants of RGC survival and death, at least in NMDA-induced retinal injury.

In addition to the cell death-promoting genes, we identified 3 more promising genes as intrinsic neuroprotective mechanisms in both the axotomy and NMDA models. First, both types of retinal injury dramatically upregulate the Edn2 gene, which encodes a nonselective endothelin A and B receptor agonistic peptide and is known as a general retinal stress response68–70. The nonselective endothelin receptor antagonist PD145065 did not affect NMDA-induced retinal injury, and the endothelin receptor B agonist sarafotoxin S6c only mildly suppressed it, suggesting its limited intrinsic neuroprotective role. Second, the Psmb9 gene was upregulated in both models, and the proteasome inhibitor MG-262 significantly exacerbated NMDA-induced retinal damage. This finding is consistent with our previous finding that all tested proteasome inhibitors, including MG-262, caused inner retinal degeneration, when given alone even in the absence of NMDA35. Furthermore, impaired proteasome function due to overexpression of a proteasome beta 5 subunit was reported to cause photoreceptor degeneration71, whereas increased proteasome activity promoted photoreceptor survival in an inherited retinal degeneration model72. These results suggest that the proteasome system contributes to retinal cell survival under both normal and disease conditions, supporting its intrinsic neuroprotective role. Finally, the Gal gene is upregulated in response to axotomy and NMDA27,34,73. Galanin is a neuropeptide expressed widely in peripheral nerves as well as in the central nervous system74, including the retina75, whose gene expression is upregulated in response to mechanical retinal injury27,34,73. Although galanin is a neurotrophic factor that promotes neuronal cell survival76 and neurite outgrowth77, its retinal role had been only speculative20. Recently, the Gal gene exogenously delivered and overexpressed via an adeno-associated virus 2 vector was shown to promote RGC survival and axonal regeneration in an optic nerve crush model78. In our study, the nonselective galanin receptor antagonist M35 exacerbated NMDA-induced retinal damage. Because M35 could be an agonist or antagonist depending on its concentration79, our finding suggests the functional significance of the upregulated Gal gene in the regulation of retinal cell survival and death as either an intrinsic neuroprotective as seen in the earlier study or cell-death promoting factor. Further studies are underway to determine its more exact role in the common cell death-promoting machinery between axotomy- and NMDA-induced retinal injury.

In conclusion, the present study delineated the time-resolved gene expression profiles in both axotomy- and NMDA-induced retinal injury models, resulting in the identification of key common networks associated with multiple molecular functions, including kinase-phosphatase, cytokine and growth factor, proteasome and galanin signaling pathways. We also demonstrated that these networks are functionally significant and may contribute at least partly to the regulation of retinal cell death and survival. Given that only a small fraction of the commonly differentially expressed genes were functionally tested in this study, more complex and dynamic interactions among all identified genes ultimately determine the fate of retinal neuronal cells, including RGCs, in those models. Further studies are underway to test the functional roles of the remaining common genes and delineate the common cell death-promoting pathways leading to RGC apoptosis for the development of novel therapeutic approaches for the treatment of optic neuropathies.

sec.title: Animals and surgical procedures
sec.p: Male Sprague-Dawley rats (7–8 weeks old, Japan SLC, Inc., Hamamatsu, Japan) were maintained at 23 ± 3 °C with a 12-hour light/12-hour dark cycle and allowed food and water ad libitum. Under anesthesia with inhaled isoflurane (3.5% for induction and 2.5% for maintenance), the optic nerve of the left eye was exposed through a small incision in the conjunctiva, and the right eye was left intact. In the axotomy group, the optic nerve was then cut with a fine surgical knife 1.5 mm distal to the globe, whereas it was left uncut in the sham-operation group. For optic nerve crush, the exposed optic nerve was mechanically injured with calibrated forceps. The maintenance of retinal circulation was confirmed by microscopic observation after each surgery. Intravitreal injection of NMDA and vehicle (PBS) was performed as described elsewhere7,35. Following axotomy and NMDA injection, the animals were sacrificed with an excess dose of pentobarbital, the eyes were enucleated, and the retinas were isolated at 6 and 12 h and 1, 3, 7, 14 and 28 days. In parallel, samples were also prepared for the normal control (0 and 28 days) and the sham and vehicle groups (6 h, 7 days and 28 days). These samples were subjected to microarray analysis and real-time PCR as described below.

To analyze the biological functions of the identified genes, small chemical inhibitors/activators, proteins and antibodies were intravitreally injected into the eyes of the rats concurrently with NMDA as described elsewhere7,35. For other target genes, knockout and knock-in mice were used. Knockout mice for C380, Fcgr381, Il1b82, B2m83 and Abb84 were obtained from Jackson Lab (Bar Harbor, ME, USA, JAX stock #003641 B6.129S4-C3tm1Crr/J and JAX stock #003171 B6.129P2-Fcgrtm1sjv/J), and Taconic (Rensselaer, NY, USA, Model #000612-M H2r-IL1βtm1Lvp, #B2MN12 B6.129-B2mtm1Jae N12 and #ABBN12 B6.129-H2-Ab1tm1Gru N12) and knock-in mice for Gp130 (gp130F759/F759)85 were obtained from Shimizu Jikken Zairyo (Kyoto, Japan). In accordance with the provider’s instructions, the recommended wild-type animals were used as the controls for the knockout mice described above. These mice were housed in the same manner as described above and anesthetized with an intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital. Following pupil dilation with tropicamide and phenylephrine hydrochloride (Mydrin-P, Santen Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., Osaka, Japan), a 2-µl aliquot of NMDA solution (5 and 10 mM) was injected into the vitreous body of the left eye through a Hamilton syringe (Hamilton Company, Reno, NV, USA) with a 33-gauge needle under a microscope. The fellow eye of each animal was uninjected and served as a control. At each designated time point following intravitreal injection of chemicals and antibodies, the rat and mouse retinas were isolated and subjected to further assays as described in the sections below.

sec.title: RNA extraction and microarray hybridization
sec.p: As described previously7,35, total RNA was extracted from the retinas via an RNeasy Mini or 96 Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The isolated retinas from animals assigned to each group were combined, resulting in pooled total RNA used for microarray hybridization as the representative sample. Fluorescein-labeled cRNAs (cyanine 3 and 5, Agilent Low RNA Input Fluorescent Linear Amplification Kit, catalog #G4140-90050, Agilent Technologies Inc., Palo Alto, CA, USA) were prepared and hybridized to Agilent rat oligo microarrays (catalog #011868 G4130A) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Briefly, following an RNA quality check via an Agilent 2100 bioanalyzer, 0.5 µg of total RNA was reverse-transcribed into a 20 µl reaction mixture containing MMLV reverse transcriptase, oligo-(d)T-T7 promoter primer, dNTPs and DTT. The resulting double-strand cDNA was transcribed and labeled with either cyanine 3 or 5 in an 80-µl reaction mixture containing cyanine 3-CTP or 5-CTP, DTT, NTP mix, PEG, inorganic pyrophosphatase and T7 RNA polymerase. Labeled cRNA was purified through an RNeasy Mini column, and its quality was checked via a bioanalyzer. Cy3-labeled cRNAs derived from a retinal total RNA sample and Cy5-labeled cRNAs derived from a reference sample (a mixture of retinal and brain total RNA) were mixed and hybridized to the same array on a glass slide assembled in an Agilent hybridization chamber (catalog #G2531). For array hybridization, 3 technical replicates were obtained for each group, where the labeling dyes were swapped between Cy3 and Cy5 in one replicate to minimize dye bias. Each array was washed sequentially in wash solutions 1 (6x SSC, 0.005% Triton X-102) and 2 (0.1x SSC, 0.005% Triton X-102), and further washed in wash solution 3 for array stabilization and drying in some experiments. The slides were scanned with an Agilent dual-laser microarray scanner (catalog #G2565AA), and each spot intensity was quantified via feature extraction software (Ver A.6.1.1).

sec.title: Microarray data analysis
sec.p: All the quantitative data for the microarray spot intensities were uploaded into GeneSpring GX version 14.9 software (Agilent Technologies Inc, Palo Alto, CA, USA). Each intensity derived from the retinal samples was normalized to that from the reference sample on the same array and each ratio was transformed into a log scale. The log ratios were further normalized to the median values on time 0 (day 0) in the normal group to minimize signal variabilities among all arrays. To identify differentially expressed genes between day 0 in the normal group and the other designated time points in the axotomy or NMDA group, ANOVA was performed, with a cutoff of P < 0.05. Neither the ad-hoc multiple comparison test nor the fold change cutoff was used to maximize the likelihood of identifying biologically meaningful genes. For differentially expressed genes, Venn diagram analysis was performed to extract overlapping genes between the axotomy and NMDA datasets, which were considered as common genes. Hierarchical and k-means clustering was used to analyze the time-resolved expression profiles of the common genes. Unbiased two- (for all samples and gene entities) and one-dimensional hierarchical clustering (only for gene entities with fixed time points) were performed to detect variabilities among 3 replicate samples at each time point and the temporal patterns of the expression of the common genes, respectively. For k-means clustering, 12 clusters were arbitrarily chosen and visually inspected to identify unique temporal profiles. On the basis of the inspected profiles, these clusters were further grouped into 5 combined clusters, namely, early, intermediate and late upregulated clusters and early and late downregulated clusters.

The common genes in the axotomy and NMDA datasets were further analyzed via Qiagen IPA (Hilden, Germany) to predict their biological significance in RGC cell survival and death, according to the manufacturer’s instructions32. Briefly, to annotate these genes, gene identifiers (array probe numbers and GenBank accession numbers) and their expression values were uploaded into IPA. These gene identifiers were automatically mapped to their corresponding gene objects in PKB, and relevant annotation data were retrieved. The common genes identified in each combined cluster were annotated with molecular features, canonical pathways and molecular and cellular functions. To determine the associations of these common genes with predefined pathways and functions in PKB, a right-tailed Fisher’s exact test was performed, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. For each combined cluster, the top 5 canonical pathways and molecular functions associated statistically significantly with the common genes were chosen for visualization.

Molecular networks were also generated via IPA to predict the interactions among the common genes and their encoded proteins in each combined cluster. The common genes were overlaid onto a global network that was generated by existing information about molecular interactions such as activation, inhibition and binding in PKB. A right-tailed Fisher’s exact test was performed for statistical significance in the enrichment of a group of genes in a given global network. Furthermore, Z scores were used for prediction of the state of molecular interactions by determining the consistency between the observed expression data and literature-based prediction. If the z score was equal to or greater than 2, the interaction was predicted to be activated, whereas if it was equal to or lower than − 2, it was deemed inhibited.

sec.title: Real-time PCR
sec.p: The detailed procedures have already been reported elsewhere7,35. Briefly, for validation of the microarray data, 9 genes (Gfap, Nefl, Clu, Prph1, Tnfrsf 1a, Arg1, C3, Usp18 and Ania4) were arbitrarily chosen. First strand cDNA (derived from the same sample RNA used for microarrays) was prepared via MMLV reverse transcriptase (Thermo Fisher Scientific Invitrogen, Waltham, MA, USA), and an aliquot of the resulting cDNA was amplified via QuantiTect SYBR Green (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) in an ABI Prism 7000 Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems, Waltham, MA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. The expression levels of each target gene were quantified via a standard curve in which a reference cDNA sample in serial dilutions (derived from the same reference RNA used for microarrays) was amplified with gene-specific primers. Each expression level was normalized to that of Gapdh in each sample and expressed relative to that observed at time 0 in the normal group. To analyze the biological functions of the common genes via the use of chemicals and antibodies, real-time PCR was performed via the ExScript RT Reagent Kit (Perfect Real Time, Takara, Shiga, Japan) and SYBR Premix Ex Taq (Takara, Shiga, Japan) in a 7500 Fast Real-Time PCR system (Applied Biosystems, Waltham, MA). The Nefl expression levels were quantified in the same manner as above and normalized to those of Rn18s. The sequences of the primers used for those genes are shown in Supplementary Table S3. For some experiments, the PrimeScript RT Reagent Kit (Takara, Shiga, Japan) and QuantiTect Multiplex PCR Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) were used for cDNA synthesis and real-time PCR, respectively. For real-time PCR, a predesigned primer-probe mixture for Gapdh (Applied Biosystems, Waltham, MA) or Nefl (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) was used as previously described7,35. The comparative CT method was used to determine Nefl expression relative to Gapdh expression, which was further normalized to that in the vehicle-treated control group.

sec.title: Histological evaluation
sec.p: For mouse33 and rat eyes7,35, the detailed procedures were described previously. Briefly, the isolated eyes were fixed in a paraformaldehyde-glutaraldehyde mixture, embedded in paraffin and cross-sectioned. Eight 3-µm retinal sections were prepared for each eye, and digital images were captured with a fully automated digital slide scanner (NanoZoomer Digital Pathology™, Hamamatsu Photonics K., Shizuoka, Japan). Three retinas were arbitrarily chosen, and the number of cells in the GCL and the thickness of the IPL were determined. For each retina, the representative value averaged across 3 sections was obtained for each parameter.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Each value represents the mean ± standard deviation. All the statistical procedures were performed via GraphPad Prism software (ver 9.3.1, GraphPad Software, San Diego, CA, USA). A linear regression analysis was performed to determine the correlation between gene expression levels obtained via microarray analysis and real-time PCR. For knockout mice, a two-tailed paired t-test was used to compare values between the right and left eyes, whereas an F-test followed by a two-tailed unpaired t-test with or without Welch’s correction was used to compare ratios of the number of cells in the GCL or the IPL thickness between wild-type and homozygous mice. For comparisons among 3 or more groups, Bartlett’s test was performed followed by ANOVA. If significant, post hoc analysis was performed via Tukey’s multiple comparison test among all groups. When Bartlett’s test determined unequal variances, Brown-Forsythe and Dunnett’s T3 test were performed instead. Differences were assumed to be statistically significant when P < 0.05.
